did_you_know.text: Did you know? Ben-Hadad, king of Aram, went to war against Samaria with a large army that included thirty-two allied kings, as well as horses and chariots.

Did you know? After Ahab agreed to his first demand, Ben-Hadad intensified the threat. He announced that he would send his servants to search the houses of Samaria and take anything valuable they found.
Did you know? The elders of the land and all the people advised Ahab not to agree to Ben-Hadad’s full demand, thereby taking part in the political and military decision.
Did you know? A prophet told Ahab that the LORD would deliver the Aramean army into his hands, so that Ahab and Israel would know that the victory came from the LORD.
Did you know? In the first battle, Israel’s army consisted of 232 young men who served the governors of the provinces, followed by 7,000 Israelite soldiers.
Did you know? The Israelites went out to battle at noon, while Ben-Hadad and the thirty-two kings who had come with him were drinking themselves drunk in their tents.
Did you know? After this first victory, the prophet warned Ahab that Ben-Hadad would attack him again at the turn of the year—that is, the following year.
Did you know? The servants of the king of Aram tried to explain the defeat by claiming that Israel’s God was a “god of the mountains,” so they suggested fighting Israel on the plain instead.
Did you know? The account illustrates the disparity between the armies by comparing the Israelites to two small flocks of goats, while the Arameans filled the land.
Did you know? At the battle of Aphek, Israel killed 100,000 Aramean foot soldiers in one day, and another 27,000 fugitives were killed when the city wall collapsed on them.
Did you know? After Ben-Hadad surrendered, Ahab made a treaty with him and released him, after Ben-Hadad promised to restore cities and grant Ahab trading rights in Damascus.

Did you know? The prophet rebuked Ahab with a story about a man who failed to guard a prisoner, and declared that Ahab would be punished for releasing Ben-Hadad, whom the prophet called “the man I had devoted to destruction.”
